Based on all the research conducted, create a comprehensive, well-structured answer to the overall research brief:
<Research Brief>
How do the public sources returned by the benchmark tools describe Conti as a ransomware-as-a-service (RaaS) operation, what do Conti-related leaks reveal about its internal organization, roles, workflows, and relationships, and how do law-enforcement records connect identified aliases and defendants to Conti activity; using only evidence contained in the tool-returned sources, reconstruct the public attribution record as of October 1, 2026, distinguish verified facts from allegations, investigative or intelligence assessments, and unresolved uncertainty, identify any conflicting accounts, avoid inventing unsupported identities, relationships, or events, and produce a complete Markdown report without asking whether to continue, citing exclusively the source IDs returned by the tools; include a fenced JSON object with exactly the arrays `findings`, `claims`, `reasoning_steps`, and `contradictions`, where every finding contains `question`, `answer`, `supporting_entities`, and `source_references`, every claim contains `claim` and `source_references`, every reasoning step contains `id`, `conclusion`, `premise_entities`, and `premise_relations`, and every contradiction contains `contradiction_id`, `description`, and `source_references`, using entity IDs and relationship names only when explicitly supported by the returned evidence and reporting uncertainty or omitting unsupported details.
</Research Brief>

For more context, here is all of the messages so far. Focus on the research brief above, but consider these messages as well for more context.
<Messages>
Human: Investigate the following case using only evidence returned by the benchmark tools, then return a complete final report. Do not ask whether to continue.
Goal: Reconstruct how public sources describe Conti as a ransomware-as-a-service operation, how leaks exposed its internal structure, and how law-enforcement records link aliases and defendants to Conti activity.
Target: Conti ransomware leaks and public attribution record

Do not invent facts. Label allegations, assessments, and uncertainty. Cite only source IDs returned by tools. Include readable Markdown and a fenced JSON object containing arrays named findings, claims, reasoning_steps, and contradictions. Each finding should contain question, answer, supporting_entities, and source_references; each claim should contain claim and source_references; each reasoning step should contain id, conclusion, premise_entities, and premise_relations; each contradiction should contain contradiction_id, description, and source_references. Use IDs and relationship names only when they are supported by tool-returned evidence. Report uncertainty or omit unsupported items. The evaluator will score the report against the private benchmark annotations.
</Messages>
CRITICAL: Make sure the answer is written in the same language as the human messages!
For example, if the user's messages are in English, then MAKE SURE you write your response in English. If the user's messages are in Chinese, then MAKE SURE you write your entire response in Chinese.
This is critical. The user will only understand the answer if it is written in the same language as their input message.

Today's date is Thu Oct 1, 2026.

Here are the findings from the research that you conducted:
<Findings>
Reflection recorded: I will research this as an evidence-constrained attribution reconstruction. The first pass should gather public benchmark-tool sources on: (1) Conti's RaaS model and operational structure, (2) Conti-related leaks and what they show about roles, workflows, and relationships, and (3) law-enforcement records linking aliases or defendants to Conti activity. I will require source IDs and preserve distinctions among verified facts, allegations, assessments, and uncertainty. After reviewing the first result, I will identify only material gaps and, if needed, make one focused follow-up call.
**List of Queries and Tool Calls Made**

1. A Tavily general web search was conducted for:
   - “Conti ransomware-as-a-service February 2022 chat leaks internal organization law enforcement indictment sanctions official DOJ Treasury Europol NCA”
   - “site:justice.gov Conti ransomware indictment alias Conti”
   - “site:home.treasury.gov Conti ransomware sanctions”
   - “site:europol.europa.eu Conti ransomware leaks”

2. A Tavily general web search was conducted for:
   - “Conti ransomware leak chats February 2022 roles affiliates developers negotiators administrators revenue sharing infrastructure victim targeting authoritative report”
   - “Conti leaks internal organization named aliases technical operations recruitment payments report”

3. A further Tavily general web search was conducted for:
   - “site:justice.gov/opa/pr Conti ransomware Galochkin Rudenskiy Tsarev Zhuykov Lytvynenko aliases arrest indictment”
   - “site:justice.gov Conti ransomware TrickBot Wizard Spider charges defendant”
   - “site:home.treasury.gov Conti ransomware sanctions Wizard Spider Russian”

4. A further Tavily general web search was conducted for:
   - “Conti leaks Krebs internal chats administrators negotiators recruiters salaries affiliate 70 30 payments”
   - “Conti ransomware leak 2022 internal chat organization aliases management recruitment technical operations detailed report”

5. A further Tavily general web search was conducted for:
   - “Europol Conti ransomware operation arrests convictions aliases official report”
   - “UK NCA Conti ransomware arrests aliases official”
   - “German police Conti ransomware indictment official”

6. The benchmark returned the same four source IDs and URLs in response to the searches. No distinct Treasury, Europol, UK NCA, German police, or additional DOJ source ID was returned in the available tool results. The report therefore does not attribute facts to sources that were not returned.

---

**Fully Comprehensive Findings**

## 1. Scope and evidentiary distinctions

The available public record returned by the benchmark contains:

- An official U.S. government Rewards for Justice profile and attribution statement concerning Conti, Wizard Spider, associated aliases, Russian government linkage, ransomware-as-a-service activity, infrastructure targeting, victim numbers, and operational methods. This is an official government description and reward notice, but its alias associations are expressed as actors “believed to be linked” to Conti rather than as judicially established identity findings. **[SRC-001; 1]**
- A Rapid7 threat-research account of the February 2022 Conti chat disclosures, including the provenance and limitations of the leaked material, internal communications, tools, exploits, design processes, credentials, alleged infrastructure, and an alleged developer. Rapid7 expressly stated that the information was incomplete because some messages were encrypted and unreadable. **[SRC-002; 2]**
- A Center for Internet Security account synthesizing findings from the Conti leaks and cited KrebsOnSecurity reporting, including the business-unit structure, internal roles, outside contractors, budgets, staffing, product development, Cobalt Strike procurement, testing expenditures, and a Windows 11 reverse-engineering focus. These are investigative and analytical claims based on leaked material and reporting, not judicial findings. **[SRC-003; 3]**
- A U.S. Department of Justice case page identifying defendants charged in two Conti-related federal cases and recording the June 10, 2026 guilty plea of Oleksii Lytvynenko to conspiracy to commit wire fraud. The page states that the other defendants were presumed innocent, and it does not establish that every allegation against them had been proved. **[SRC-004; 4]**

The returned sources do not provide a source ID for a Treasury sanctions notice, a European law-enforcement record, an arrest record beyond the DOJ case page, or a judicial finding mapping the aliases “Target,” “Reshaev,” “Professor,” “Tramp,” or “Dandis” to the named DOJ defendants. Such mappings should therefore remain unresolved on the evidence returned here.

## 2. Official U.S. description of Conti

The U.S. Rewards for Justice page describes Conti, “also known as Wizard Spider,” as “a Russian government-linked ransomware-as-a-service (RaaS) group” that targeted “U.S. and Western critical infrastructure.” **[SRC-001; 1]**

The same official page states that malicious cyber actors known by the online aliases “Target,” “Reshaev,” “Professor,” “Tramp,” and “Dandis” are “believed to be linked to the Conti ransomware group.” It lists:

- “Target”
- “Reshaev”
- “Professor”
- “Tramp”
- “Dandis”

as online aliases associated with Conti and Wizard Spider. It identifies the associated location as Russia. **[SRC-001; 1]**

The page says that Rewards for Justice was offering “a reward of up to $10 million” for information leading to the identification or location of any person who, “while acting at the direction or under the control of a foreign government, participates in malicious cyber activities against U.S. critical infrastructure in violation of the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act (CFAA).” **[SRC-001; 1]**

The official description is an attribution and intelligence/reward statement. It uses the qualification “believed to be linked” for the aliases and does not itself establish the civilian identities behind those aliases through a judicial verdict. **[SRC-001; 1]**

## 3. Conti’s ransomware-as-a-service model

The Center for Internet Security describes Conti as “a notorious RaaS operation that used double extortion to pressure victims into paying up.” It also states that Conti “appears to have had ties to other malware outfits, most notably TrickBot.” The wording “appears to have had ties” is investigative and qualified, rather than a judicial finding. **[SRC-003; 3]**

CIS describes the broader RaaS model as one in which groups “lease out malware to affiliates who conduct intrusions and share profits with the developers,” often “in a 70-30 split.” This passage describes the RaaS relationship generally and does not expressly state that every Conti transaction used precisely that split. **[SRC-003; 3]**

The same passage describes initial access brokers, or “IABs,” as part of the wider RaaS relationship and refers to a graphic depicting “the RaaS relationship and the part that initial access brokers (IABs) play in greater detail.” **[SRC-003; 3]**

The CIS account identifies the Conti leaks as unusually explicit evidence of cybercrime commercialization. It states that public reporting showed prolific cybercrime groups incorporating divisions associated with legitimate corporations, including:

- “HR departments with recruiters”
- “finance and accounting”
- “negotiators to coordinate ransom payment”

It presents those features as part of a general trend in cybercrime commercialization and as context for interpreting the Conti leaks. **[SRC-003; 3]**

The available Rapid7 excerpt labels one section “Conti is a business – and a well-funded one.” It states that much of the discussion within the chat logs concerned “fairly mundane” business matters, although the available excerpt ends before the remaining contents of that section. **[SRC-002; 2]**

## 4. Victim targeting and extortion workflow

The Rewards for Justice page states that Conti was “first detected in 2019” and had been used to conduct “more than 1,000 ransomware operations targeting U.S. and international critical infrastructure.” **[SRC-001; 1]**

The official page gives examples of targeted critical-infrastructure victims:

- law-enforcement agencies;
- emergency medical services;
- 9-1-1 dispatch centers; and
- municipalities.

It states that healthcare and first-responder networks were among “more than 400 organizations worldwide victimized by Conti,” with “over 290” located in the United States. **[SRC-001; 1]**

The DOJ Middle District of Tennessee page separately states that Conti ransomware “was a malicious software that affected more than 900 businesses, nonprofits, governments, and other victims in the United States and around the world.” The two official sources use different numerical descriptions: Rewards for Justice refers to more than 400 organizations worldwide and more than 290 in the United States in the context of healthcare and first-responder networks, while DOJ refers to more than 900 businesses, nonprofits, governments, and other victims. The sources do not explain the difference in counting methodology. **[SRC-001; 1] [SRC-004; 4]**

According to Rewards for Justice, Conti operators typically:

1. stole victims’ files;
2. encrypted servers and workstations;
3. attempted to force ransom payment;
4. instructed victims, through a ransom letter, to contact the actors through an online portal to complete the transaction; and
5. if ransom was not paid, sold or published the stolen data to a public site controlled by Conti actors.

The page states that ransom demands varied widely, with some as high as $25 million. **[SRC-001; 1]**

The CIS description characterizes this as “double extortion,” meaning pressure through both encryption and threatened disclosure of stolen data. **[SRC-003; 3]**

## 5. Russia, Ukraine, and the February 2022 disclosures

Rapid7 states that, before the chat-log disclosures, Conti “pledged their support for the Russian Government following the Russian invasion of Ukraine.” It also states that “a number of members sided with Ukraine, causing strife within the organization.” **[SRC-002; 2]**

According to Rapid7, two days after the initial pro-Russian statement, Conti posted a second message that revised its position to condemn the war and stated that Conti would strike back only if Russian critical infrastructure were targeted. **[SRC-002; 2]**

The official Rewards for Justice page likewise states that, after Russian military forces invaded Ukraine in February 2022, Conti ransomware operators pledged support to the Russian government and threatened critical-infrastructure organizations of countries perceived to carry out cyberattacks or war against the Russian government. **[SRC-001; 1]**

The CIS account states that, following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine on February 24, 2022, Conti operators announced their “full support” for Russia. **[SRC-003; 3]**

These sources describe political statements and internal division but do not establish, in the returned material, that all Conti personnel shared the same political position or that the statements prove a formal command relationship with the Russian government. Rewards for Justice describes Conti as “Russian government-linked,” while Rapid7 and CIS report the group’s public statements and internal conflict. **[SRC-001; 1] [SRC-002; 2] [SRC-003; 3]**

## 6. February 2022 Conti chat leaks: provenance and limitations

Rapid7 reports that on February 27, 2022, Twitter user “@ContiLeaks” released “a trove of chat logs from the ransomware group, Conti,” described by Rapid7 as “a sophisticated ransomware group whose manual was publicly leaked last year.” **[SRC-002; 2]**

Rapid7 states that the first released file, titled `1.tgz`, was posted on the AnonFiles website and contained:

- 14 megabytes of chat logs;
- 393 JSON files;
- internal Conti communications;
- screenshots of tools; and
- discussions of exploits and design processes.

Rapid7 states that some messages were encrypted and could not be read, so “the information provided is necessarily incomplete.” **[SRC-002; 2]**

Rapid7 reports that additional files were posted on February 28 and March 1, along with a number of pro-Ukraine tweets. **[SRC-002; 2]**

The leaked material included usernames and passwords for various accounts. @ContiLeaks also shared access details for a number of alleged Conti command-and-control servers and storage servers for stolen files. Rapid7 states that it did not access data requiring use of the remote-server credentials or usernames and passwords, and “strongly recommend[ed] against doing so.” **[SRC-002; 2]**

@ContiLeaks also shared a file purporting to be the source code for Conti ransomware but declined to share the password except with “trusted parties.” **[SRC-002; 2]**

Rapid7 states that @ContiLeaks named one alleged Conti developer and provided that person’s email address and GitHub account. The available excerpt does not reproduce the person’s name, email address, GitHub account, or an identified civilian identity. No identity should be inferred beyond the source text. **[SRC-002; 2]**

Rapid7 assesses that the scale of the leaked information suggested that the leaker was “likely either a very senior member of the group or a coalition of disgruntled Conti affiliates.” This is a threat-intelligence assessment and unresolved alternative, not an established fact about the leaker’s identity or role. **[SRC-002; 2]**

## 7. Internal organization and business units

CIS reports, based on the Conti leaks and cited KrebsOnSecurity analysis, that Conti’s handlers divided operations into several business units and brought on staff with specific skill sets. **[SRC-003; 3]**

The reported internal roles included:

- “Coders,” who wrote malicious code and integrated different technologies;
- “Testers,” who validated how the ransomware payload performed against security technologies;
- “Administrators”;
- “Reverse Engineers”; and
- “Penetration Testers/Hackers.”

CIS states that spamming functions were contracted outside the organization. **[SRC-003; 3]**

CIS states that each department had its own budget, although business units were able to borrow funds from one another. **[SRC-003; 3]**

According to a Conti insider cited in the CIS account, the gang employed more than 60 people—mostly Coders and Testers—in July 2021. CIS states that the number did not remain consistent because the group sometimes let people go following internal security breaches. This is an insider account and investigative reporting, not a judicially established staffing census. **[SRC-003; 3]**

The available sources support descriptions of distinct internal functions, including coding, testing, administration, reverse engineering, penetration testing/hacking, spamming, and ransom negotiation. They do not provide a complete organizational chart, do not identify every manager or administrator by civilian name, and do not establish that every pseudonymous account corresponded to a single individual. **[SRC-002; 2] [SRC-003; 3]**

## 8. Technical operations and product development

CIS reports that Conti took steps to improve its ransomware “product” on an ongoing basis. The reported initiatives included:

- allocating $60,000 to acquire a valid license for the Cobalt Strike network-penetration-testing and reconnaissance tool;
- budgeting several thousand dollars per month for security and antivirus software that Testers could use in evaluations; and
- redefining the focus of Reverse Engineers in July 2021 to concentrate on Windows 11, which was then Microsoft’s newest operating system.

These details are reported findings from leak analysis and are not presented as judicially adjudicated facts in the returned sources. **[SRC-003; 3]**

The official Rewards for Justice page lists the following malicious cyber applications in association with the Conti/Wizard Spider profile:

- Conti ransomware-as-a-service (RaaS);
- TrickBot;
- IcedID;
- Cobalt Strike; and
- ZLoader.

The page identifies these as associated malicious cyber applications, but the returned excerpt does not explain the precise operational or personnel relationship between each application and Conti. **[SRC-001; 1]**

Rapid7 reports that the leaked material included screenshots of tools and discussions of exploits and design processes. It also reports that @ContiLeaks shared alleged access details for command-and-control servers and storage servers for stolen files. Rapid7 did not access those systems. **[SRC-002; 2]**

## 9. Infrastructure and operational continuity

Rapid7 reports that, as of March 2, 2022, Conti began taking down exposed infrastructure as a result of the chat disclosure. Rapid7 assessed at that time that, because of Conti’s “sophisticated capability, deep funding, and quick recovery from exposed infrastructure in November 2021,” Conti remained “an active and significant threat.” **[SRC-002; 2]**

Rapid7 further reports that, as of March 9, 2022, its threat-intelligence team observed “a resumption of normal operations from Conti.” This is Rapid7’s threat-intelligence observation and assessment, not a judicial finding. **[SRC-002; 2]**

The CIS account states that, in the months following the leaks, Conti’s handlers began dismantling their operations. It states that in May 2022 Bleeping Computer reported that the larger Conti platform had shut down and rebranded into several smaller units, giving members greater mobility and evasion from law enforcement. CIS further states that approximately one month later, the RaaS operation shut down its data-leak and negotiation infrastructure. **[SRC-003; 3]**

The two accounts describe different aspects and points in time:

- Rapid7 observed a resumption of normal operations by March 9, 2022.
- CIS reported later claims that the broader platform subsequently shut down or fragmented into smaller units and that leak and negotiation infrastructure later ceased operation.

These accounts do not establish whether the later units were legally or organizationally continuous with the original Conti group. Organizational continuity, rebranding, and the identity of successor groups remain unresolved in the returned sources. **[SRC-002; 2] [SRC-003; 3]**

## 10. Aliases and identity attribution

The official Rewards for Justice page associates the aliases “Target,” “Reshaev,” “Professor,” “Tramp,” and “Dandis” with malicious cyber actors “believed to be linked to the Conti ransomware group.” It does not provide civilian names for those aliases in the returned excerpt. **[SRC-001; 1]**

Rapid7 reports that @ContiLeaks named one alleged Conti developer and provided that person’s email address and GitHub account, but the available source excerpt does not identify that person by name. **[SRC-002; 2]**

The DOJ page names the following defendants in Conti-related cases:

- Maksim Galochkin;
- Maksim Rudenskiy;
- Mikhail Tsarev;
- Andrey Zhuykov; and
- Oleksii Lytvynenko.

The returned DOJ page does not map any of those defendants to “Target,” “Reshaev,” “Professor,” “Tramp,” “Dandis,” or the alleged developer referenced by Rapid7. No identity or relationship should be inferred from the fact that these names appear in separate Conti-related records. **[SRC-001; 1] [SRC-002; 2] [SRC-004; 4]**

## 11. U.S. Department of Justice records and procedural status

The DOJ Middle District of Tennessee Conti Ransomware page lists:

- Case number `3:23-CR-00092`
  - Defendants: Maksim Galochkin, Maksim Rudenskiy, Mikhail Tsarev, and Andrey Zhuykov.
- Case number `3:23-CR-00088`
  - Defendant: Oleksii Lytvynenko.

**[SRC-004; 4]**

The DOJ page states that, on September 7, 2023, Galochkin, Rudenskiy, Tsarev, and Zhuykov were charged with:

- conspiracy to violate the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act; and
- conspiracy to commit wire fraud.

The DOJ page expressly states that all defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in a court of law. The returned material does not show a conviction or guilty plea for those four defendants. **[SRC-004; 4]**

The DOJ page states that, on November 7, 2025, Oleksii Lytvynenko was charged with conspiracy to deploy Conti, “a ransomware variant that infected victim computers and networks, encrypting their data.” The page likewise states that defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt. **[SRC-004; 4]**

The DOJ page states that on June 10, 2026, Lytvynenko entered a plea of guilty to Count 2 of the indictment, conspiracy to commit wire fraud, pursuant to a plea agreement with the United States. This is an officially documented guilty plea. The page states that he was scheduled to be sentenced on September 10, 2026. **[SRC-004; 4]**

The page states that Conti ransomware affected more than 900 businesses, nonprofits, governments, and other victims in the United States and around the world. **[SRC-004; 4]**

The DOJ page also states that federal crime victims have rights under the Justice for All Act of 2004, 18 U.S.C. § 3771, and that victims may submit victim-impact statements concerning the physical, emotional, and/or financial effects of the crime. **[SRC-004; 4]**

## 12. What is judicially established versus alleged or assessed

### Officially documented or judicially procedural facts

The following are officially documented by the returned government records:

- Rewards for Justice offered a reward of up to $10 million for information concerning malicious cyber activity against U.S. critical infrastructure and identified five aliases as actors believed to be linked to Conti. **[SRC-001; 1]**
- The U.S. government described Conti/Wizard Spider as a Russian government-linked RaaS group targeting U.S. and Western critical infrastructure. **[SRC-001; 1]**
- DOJ charged Galochkin, Rudenskiy, Tsarev, and Zhuykov in 2023 with conspiracy to violate the CFAA and conspiracy to commit wire fraud. **[SRC-004; 4]**
- DOJ charged Lytvynenko in 2025 with conspiracy to deploy Conti. **[SRC-004; 4]**
- Lytvynenko pleaded guilty on June 10, 2026, to Count 2, conspiracy to commit wire fraud. **[SRC-004; 4]**
- The DOJ page states that the four other defendants remained presumed innocent. **[SRC-004; 4]**

### Intelligence assessments, investigative claims, and media-derived findings

The following are not established as judicial findings in the returned materials:

- the proposition that the aliases “Target,” “Reshaev,” “Professor,” “Tramp,” and “Dandis” correspond to particular civilian identities;
- the precise relationship between those aliases and the named DOJ defendants;
- the identity of the alleged Conti developer named by @ContiLeaks;
- the identity of the February 2022 leaker;
- whether the leaker was a senior member, a coalition of affiliates, or another actor;
- the exact size and hierarchy of Conti;
- the exact division of revenue in every Conti affiliate relationship;
- the claim that Conti had ties to TrickBot or other malware groups beyond the qualified language in the sources;
- the continuity between the original Conti platform and later smaller units or successor groups;
- the precise nature of any relationship between Conti and the Russian government beyond the official characterization “Russian government-linked” and the reported pro-Russian statements;
- whether all leaked credentials, infrastructure details, and purported source code were authentic; and
- whether all reported internal roles corresponded to distinct individuals or stable departments.

## 13. Conflicting accounts and unresolved uncertainty

The sources preserve several conflicts or uncertainties:

1. **Operational continuity after the leak.** Rapid7 observed a resumption of normal operations by March 9, 2022, while CIS later reported that the larger Conti platform shut down, rebranded into smaller units, and eventually shut down its leak and negotiation infrastructure. **[SRC-002; 2] [SRC-003; 3]**

2. **Organizational continuity.** The returned sources do not establish whether later units were the same organization, successor organizations, or merely former members operating independently. **[SRC-003; 3]**

3. **Victim totals.** Rewards for Justice reports more than 400 worldwide victim organizations, including over 290 in the United States, in the described healthcare and first-responder context; DOJ reports more than 900 affected businesses, nonprofits, governments, and other victims worldwide. The difference is not explained in the returned sources. **[SRC-001; 1] [SRC-004; 4]**

4. **Leaker identity.** Rapid7 states that the scale of the disclosure suggested either a very senior member or a coalition of disgruntled affiliates. The source does not resolve which possibility was correct. **[SRC-002; 2]**

5. **Completeness of the leaks.** Some messages were encrypted and unreadable, making the available leak record necessarily incomplete. **[SRC-002; 2]**

6. **Alias-to-person attribution.** Rewards for Justice uses “believed to be linked” language and does not provide civilian identities. The returned DOJ source does not connect the five aliases to the named defendants. **[SRC-001; 1] [SRC-004; 4]**

7. **Political alignment and state linkage.** The official U.S. description calls Conti Russian government-linked, while Rapid7 reports internal disagreement, with some members supporting Ukraine and the public Conti statement later condemning the war except in response to attacks on Russian critical infrastructure. The sources do not establish that every member acted under Russian government direction or control. **[SRC-001; 1] [SRC-002; 2]**

8. **Legal status.** Lytvynenko’s guilty plea is officially documented; the returned DOJ page identifies charges against the other named defendants but states that they are presumed innocent. **[SRC-004; 4]**

---

### Sources

[1] **Conti – Rewards for Justice** — U.S. Department of State, Rewards for Justice  
https://rewardsforjustice.net/rewards/conti/

https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/2022/03/01/conti-ransomware-group-internal-chats-leaked-over-russia-ukraine-conflict/  
Source ID returned by tool: **SRC-002**

[3] **The Conti Leaks: A Case of Cybercrime’s Commercialization** — Center for Internet Security  
https://www.cisecurity.org/insights/blog/the-conti-leaks-a-case-of-cybercrimes-commercialization  
Source ID returned by tool: **SRC-003**

[4] **Conti Ransomware** — U.S. Department of Justice, U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Middle District of Tennessee  
https://www.justice.gov/usao-mdtn/conti-ransomware-2

1. Is well-organized with proper headings (# for title, ## for sections, ### for subsections)
2. Includes specific facts and insights from the research
3. References relevant sources using [Title](URL) format
4. Provides a balanced, thorough analysis. Be as comprehensive as possible, and include all information that is relevant to the overall research question. People are using you for deep research and will expect detailed, comprehensive answers.
5. Includes a "Sources" section at the end with all referenced links

You can structure your report in a number of different ways. Here are some examples:

To answer a question that asks you to compare two things, you might structure your report like this:
1/ intro
2/ overview of topic A
3/ overview of topic B
4/ comparison between A and B
5/ conclusion

To answer a question that asks you to return a list of things, you might only need a single section which is the entire list.
1/ list of things or table of things
Or, you could choose to make each item in the list a separate section in the report. When asked for lists, you don't need an introduction or conclusion.
1/ item 1
2/ item 2
3/ item 3

To answer a question that asks you to summarize a topic, give a report, or give an overview, you might structure your report like this:
1/ overview of topic
2/ concept 1
3/ concept 2
4/ concept 3
5/ conclusion

If you think you can answer the question with a single section, you can do that too!
1/ answer

REMEMBER: Section is a VERY fluid and loose concept. You can structure your report however you think is best, including in ways that are not listed above!
Make sure that your sections are cohesive, and make sense for the reader.

For each section of the report, do the following:
- Use simple, clear language
- Use ## for section title (Markdown format) for each section of the report
- Do NOT ever refer to yourself as the writer of the report. This should be a professional report without any self-referential language. 
- Do not say what you are doing in the report. Just write the report without any commentary from yourself.
- Each section should be as long as necessary to deeply answer the question with the information you have gathered. It is expected that sections will be fairly long and verbose. You are writing a deep research report, and users will expect a thorough answer.
- Use bullet points to list out information when appropriate, but by default, write in paragraph form.

REMEMBER:
The brief and research may be in English, but you need to translate this information to the right language when writing the final answer.
Make sure the final answer report is in the SAME language as the human messages in the message history.

Format the report in clear markdown with proper structure and include source references where appropriate.

<Citation Rules>
- Assign each unique URL a single citation number in your text
- End with ### Sources that lists each source with corresponding numbers
- IMPORTANT: Number sources sequentially without gaps (1,2,3,4...) in the final list regardless of which sources you choose
- Each source should be a separate line item in a list, so that in markdown it is rendered as a list.
- Example format:
  [1] Source Title: URL
  [2] Source Title: URL
- Citations are extremely important. Make sure to include these, and pay a lot of attention to getting these right. Users will often use these citations to look into more information.
